analysis.one_liner: Restores oil, gas, and coal leasing on federal land, cuts royalties, and speeds up environmental permitting.
analysis.headline: The House Natural Resources Committee approved the bill 24-19 in March 2023, but it was never brought to the House or Senate floor and expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Interior Department to hold frequent oil and gas lease sales on federal land and offshore, including a minimum of four sales a year in each of nine states, and to grant pending coal leases. It would cut the royalties energy companies pay for extracting publicly owned oil and gas, eliminate an administrative fee, shorten environmental reviews, and make it much harder for courts to stop lease sales or drilling projects. It also increases the share of offshore energy revenue sent to coastal states and speeds up geothermal and mineral permitting.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that drill on federal land and offshore, coal companies with pending federal lease applications, and mining companies looking to speed up exploration permits. Coastal states would receive a larger share of offshore energy revenue, and geothermal developers would benefit from faster permitting.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Department to immediately resume quarterly onshore oil and gas lease sales and to hold a minimum of four lease sales per year in each state with lands available for leasing, including Wyoming, New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, Montana, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Nevada, and Alaska [S2][S3][S4].
Requires offshore sales, including at least two Gulf of Mexico lease sales per year and two Alaska-region sales annually, and mandates a 2023-2028 offshore leasing program [S4].

Reduces royalties for oil and gas development on federal land and eliminates the administrative fee under the Mineral Leasing Act, lowering the cost companies pay to extract publicly owned resources [S2][S3][S4].

Requires the Interior Department to grant pending coal lease applications and to approve additional approvals needed for mining to begin, and nullifies the 2016 Secretarial Order that paused new federal coal leasing while its environmental impacts were reviewed [S4].

Shortens and narrows environmental reviews: environmental assessments must be completed within one year and impact statements within two years, documents are capped at 75 or 150 pages, project sponsors may prepare their own reviews, and reviews for oil and gas leases cannot consider the downstream effects of burning the fuel [S4].

Makes it much harder to stop energy projects in court: lease sales generally cannot be vacated or enjoined unless a court finds imminent and substantial environmental harm, lawsuits must be filed within 120 days by people who commented during review, and injunctive relief is barred under the new NEPA process [S4].

Allows drilling and geothermal operations on land where the federal government owns less than half the minerals to proceed with a state permit alone, bypassing federal environmental review, Endangered Species Act consultation, and historic preservation review [S4].
Increases the share of Gulf of Mexico energy revenue shared with coastal states and extends the same sharing to offshore wind revenue [S2][S3][S4].
Bars the Chinese Communist Party from acquiring any interest in federal oil and gas leases [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would collect less royalty and fee revenue from oil and gas taken from publicly owned land and waters. Communities near leased public land would face drilling, mining, and infrastructure with shorter environmental reviews, less public input, and sharply limited ability to challenge projects in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and communities near public lands

drawbacks.text: Lower royalties and eliminated fees would reduce the money the federal Treasury collects from resources owned by the public, meaning ordinary taxpayers effectively subsidize extraction companies' costs [S2][S3][S4].

Narrowing environmental review to the immediate lease plot and excluding downstream effects of oil and gas consumption means the public decision-making process would no longer weigh the climate effects of the fuel being extracted [S4].

The litigation restrictions would sharply limit the ability of citizens, tribes, and conservation groups to challenge federal energy decisions in court, with a 120-day filing window, a requirement to have commented first, and a near-total bar on court orders pausing projects [S4].

Allowing sponsors to prepare their own environmental documents, capping their length, and letting companies drill on mixed-ownership land with only a state permit would reduce federal oversight of projects that affect public resources [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes genuinely popular ideas — permitting deadlines, monthly public reporting of permit backlogs, faster geothermal leasing, a bigger revenue share for coastal states, and a bar on Chinese Communist Party ownership — with its core purpose: cheaper, faster extraction of publicly owned oil, gas, and coal, paid for by lower royalties to taxpayers and weaker environmental review and judicial checks. The industry provisions dominate the bill's size and effect, so on balance its costs to the public fall on taxpayers and communities near federal energy development.

outcome.mechanism: The House Natural Resources Committee reported the bill in March 2023 and it was placed on the Union Calendar — the queue for House floor votes — but it was never brought up for a vote in the House or Senate, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 3, 2023, by Rep. Bruce Westerman and referred to the Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Budget Committees [S1][S6].
The Natural Resources Committee ordered it reported as amended by a 24-19 vote on March 9, 2023 [S6].

The committee formally reported the bill on March 23, 2023 (H. Rept. 118-28); the Agriculture and Budget Committees were discharged, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 18 [S3][S6].
No further action was taken: the bill received no vote in the full House or any action in the Senate before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers and communities near public lands are better off because the bill died: royalty rates and environmental review standards for drilling and mining on public land stayed as they were. Oil, gas, and coal companies did not get the expanded leasing access, lower royalties, and court protections the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers and communities near public lands

sides.party_line_note: The committee approved the bill 24-19; its sponsor, two original cosponsors, and both additional cosponsors were all Republicans, though the record provided does not show the party breakdown of the 24-19 committee vote.

industries.note: The bill would mandate frequent onshore and offshore lease sales, cut the royalties and fees companies pay for publicly owned resources, speed up drilling permits, and make lease sales nearly impossible to challenge in court. Because the oil and gas belongs to the public, lower royalties mean ordinary taxpayers collect less for resources extracted from their land.

The bill would force Interior to grant pending coal lease applications and approvals needed for mining to start, and would nullify the 2016 order that paused new federal coal leasing for review. Communities near mines would face expanded coal extraction with expedited environmental review.

industries.industry: Hardrock and critical mineral mining companies
industries.note: The bill would expedite mineral exploration and mine permitting, designate mining as a covered sector for federal permitting improvement, and direct consideration of uranium as a critical mineral, reducing the environmental analysis and public process before mining begins on federal land.

The same permitting streamlining would help geothermal leasing deadlines and transmission and storage projects on federal land, which is where the bill's broadest non-fossil benefit lies. These gains are secondary to the bill's fossil-focused core.

The bill would increase the share of Gulf of Mexico energy revenue going to coastal states and extend equivalent sharing to offshore wind revenue, sending more money from federal waters to state budgets.
